title: whentorebrandtriggers
claim: A rebrand is only justified when unit economics, product scope, or distribution channels fundamentally change.
hook: Knowing exactly when to rebrand saves millions in wasted agency fees and lost brand equity.

slides.headline: When to rebrand your business (and when not to)
Do not rebrand just because sales are dropping
slides.body: A decline in sales is usually a distribution or product problem. Changing your logo and color palette does not fix a broken growth loop or a weak value proposition.

slides.headline: Your customer profile changed by an order of magnitude
slides.body: If you moved from self-serve SMBs paying 50 dollars a month to enterprise accounts paying 50,000 dollars, your visual identity and messaging must reflect high-trust corporate standards.

slides.headline: Your legacy name restricts product category expansion
slides.body: When Dunkin Donuts dropped Donuts from its name in 2018, beverage sales made up 60 percent of revenue. The old name was actively suppressing their highest-margin category.

slides.headline: Your distribution channel completely flipped
slides.body: A brand designed to catch eyes on a crowded retail shelf looks chaotic on a minimalist e-commerce screen. Packaging designed for physical retail fails in digital-first environments.

slides.headline: Before hiring an agency run this simple checklist
slides.body: Ask if your product value proposition, pricing tier, or sales channel shifted in the last 12 months. If none of these changed, fix your acquisition funnel instead of your logo.

slides.headline: Send this to a founder planning a redesign
slides.body: Save this post for your next brand strategy review or forward it to a teammate currently questioning their visual identity.

caption:
Knowing exactly when to rebrand saves millions in wasted agency fees and lost brand equity.

Most corporate rebrands happen for bad reasons. An incoming marketing executive wants to leave a mark, sales dipped for two consecutive quarters, or internal teams grew bored of the visual guidelines. None of these justify altering customer recall.

A rebrand is a structural response to operational shifts. When Dunkin dropped Donuts from its name in 2018, beverage sales already accounted for 60 percent of total revenue. The operational reality had moved, and the existing name was capping margin expansion.

If your pricing tier, buyer persona, or primary acquisition channel has not changed in the past year, redesigning your identity will not solve your revenue problems.

Changing your logo when your product funnel is broken is expensive procrastination.

Send this to a founder or marketing lead currently debating a rebrand.
